item.title: PhD position in compiler verification at IT University of Copenhagen (Deadline 1 Jan 2027)
item.dc:creator: paba
item.description:
We invite applications for a fully funded 3-year PhD position at the IT University of Copenhagen (ITU), as part of the MAVERIC project (Modular Algebraic Verification of Compilers), funded by the Independent Research Fund Denmark (DFF). The position starts on 1 April 2027; a later start can be negotiated.

The Project

MAVERIC aims to make compiler verification simpler and more modular by bringing together two previously separate approaches. The first is compiler calculation, in which a compiler is proved correct step by step through equational reasoning. The second is concurrent separation logic, the gold standard for modular reasoning about concurrent programs with heap-allocated memory. The key challenge is to devise an algebraic theory in which equational reasoning is conditioned on separation-logic specifications, and to implement it in a proof assistant as a practical framework for compiler verification.

Candidate Profile

  • An MSc in computer science, mathematics, or a closely related field.
  • A solid background in programming language theory or formal verification.
  • Experience with proof assistants (e.g., Rocq, Agda, or Lean), separation logic, or compilers is an advantage, but not required.

How to Apply

  • Further details on the position and how to apply
  • Application deadline: 1 January 2027.

If you have any questions, or are unsure whether your profile fits, feel free to contact me at paba@itu.dk before applying.

item.title: Rocq-web: Rocq 9.2 and coq-lsp in the browser, with 57 packages
item.dc:creator: rboudrouss
item.description:
rocq.rboud.com

rocq-web

rocq-web is Rocq 9.2 and coq-lsp compiled to WebAssembly, running in a Web Worker fully client side.

It comes with 57 packages downloaded only when a file requires them. Among them are the standard library, Mathematical Components and analysis, Iris and stdpp, Equations, MetaRocq, Hierarchy-Builder and rocq-elpi, Flocq, Coquelicot, Interval and CoRN. Their OCaml plugins work too.

The editor works like RocqIDE. You can check step by step or as you type, see the goals and what each tactic changed, and use hover, completion, go to definition (into the libraries’ sources too), and queries like Search or About. A project can be opened from a folder on disk, a zip archive or a GitHub repository. A file can be shared as a link, and the page can be embedded in another one with ?embed.

Chrome, Edge 137+ and Firefox 153+ run the full build, with a 64-bit memory and up to 16 GB of RAM. Other browsers get a slower build limited to 4 GB.

rocq-web runs “the same” 64-bit code as a native Rocq and reads the .vo files of an opam switch as they are, so adding a package to the site only means installing it in the switch and rebuilding.

How it is built, and how to reuse it

Rocq and coq-lsp go from OCaml to C with c_of_ocaml, then to WebAssembly with emscripten, through ocaml-emcc. ocaml-emcc compiles OCaml programs together with their C stubs, so nothing has to be rewritten in JavaScript, and it builds OCaml plugins into WebAssembly side modules loaded at run time.

If you want Rocq inside your own web project, you do not need rocq-web as a dependency. You can build Rocq, coq-lsp or your own tool with ocaml-emcc directly. The Makefile of rocq-web is commented step by step and is meant as a working example.

Limitations

native_compute falls back to the VM. Libraries added by hand in the page cannot bring OCaml plugins yet, since those cannot be compiled in the browser. A heavy session can use several GB of memory (use restart button to clear it).

The code is at GitHub - rboudrouss/rocq-web · GitHub. Feedback is very welcome, especially bug reports and packages or features you would like to see added.

item.title: Nov 16, 2026: Proof Assistant Seminar at ENS de Lyon
item.dc:creator: CohenCyril
item.description:
Dear all,

It is our pleasure to announce the first session of the second year of our working group dedicated to proof assistants and their use at ENS de Lyon, one week from now. The working group will be hybrid, see the locations at the bottom of the mail.

The detailed schedule for Nov 16, 2026

with talks from Cyril Cohen, Reynald Affeldt et Alexandre Moine

10:30-12:00 Rocq Tutorial #1 (reloaded)

Cyril Cohen: an introduction to the Rocq prover.

13:30-14:45 First talk

Title: Formal verification of tilt estimation using the Rocq prover

Presenter: Reynald Affeldt (joint work with Lynda Bentoucha, Yoshihiro Ishiguro, and Holger Thies)

Abstract:

The safe operation of a humanoid robot critically relies on
accurate estimation of its vertical orientation, or “tilt”.
This requires a variety of mathematical tools, including
three-dimensional geometry and differential equations.
To formally verify tilt estimation, we develop a library
for stability analysis in the Rocq prover.
We start by formalizing a theory of ordinary differential equations.
We provide a formalization of the (local) Cauchy-Lipschitz
(a.k.a. Picard-Lindelof) theorem for existence and uniqueness,
taking advantage of the library support for quotients provided by
the Mathematical Components library.
We extend this formalization with a variant for global existence
and continuous dependence on initial conditions.
Building on these foundations, we develop a theory of Lyapunov
stability that is compatible with an existing formalization of
LaSalle’s invariance principle.
We also extend an existing library for the statics of robot
manipulators to support dynamical systems.
Finally, we apply these libraries to the verification of a
state-of-the-art tilt estimation developed for a humanoid robot.

15:00-16:15 Second talk

Title : Uncle Scrooge’s Guide to Verified Efficiency: Separation Logic with Credits in Rocq

Presenter: Alexandre Moine

Abstract:

Proving that a program computes the right result is only half the
story: we would also like to know that it does so efficiently,
without taking too long or using too much memory. In this talk,
I will show how to use (and build) program logics in Rocq that
establish such resource bounds, based on a simple idea: *credits*.
A credit is a logical token that grants permission to consume one
unit of a resource. Like Uncle Scrooge, the logic counts every
coin: programs must “pay” for every step they take or every memory
cell they allocate, so the credits a program is given bound its
resource usage.

I will start with a gentle introduction to separation logic and
to Iris, a framework for building separation logics inside Rocq.
I will show how credits can be defined as ghost state, and how
the soundness of the logic ties credits to the actual cost of an
execution. I will then present two logics from my work. The first
uses *space credits* to bound the heap space of programs under
garbage collection. The second uses *work and span credits* to
bound the time complexity of parallel programs.

Location

  • Amphi K, ENS de Lyon (site Monod), 46 allée d’Italie 69007 Lyon
  • Webinaire de l'État

Further news

Please register to the following mailing list to get information about future sessions, news and reminders:

and/or to the Zulip channel

If you want to contribute a talk, please send a mail to

item.title: SLOT: A model checker for actor-based languages with I/O
item.dc:creator: k32
item.description:
In my spare time I has been developing SLOT, a library that can be thought as a formally-verified model checker for functional actor-based languages, performing I/O with nondeterministic side effects (read: Erlang). This project is still at a relatively early stage of development, but recently I’ve achieved the first milestone: completion of the core theory.

A little bit about the design choices:

  • I/O is emulated by composable effect handlers. Users can supply their own. This differentiates it from Verdi, which comes with predefined effects related to network and disk (at least when I last checked).
  • Actors can spawn new actors
  • Optimized. The number of processes schedulings in a concurrent system grows exponentially or even faster, making brute-force approaches unfeasible. SLOT addresses this problem using a verified symmetry-reduction procedure based on “trace canonicalization” (for lack of a better term). From a set of system traces containing commuting I/O effects, SLOT selects a single one according to some rules. Any invariant proven for the canonical trace holds for any permutation of commuting events.
  • Spawning of actors commutes
  • Setoids everywhere. For example, SLOT defines event commutativity via setoid equivalence

Once again, this project is still far from being usable at this moment: I still need to develop tactics, sample I/O handlers and more, but if you are interested — discussions, reviews, feature requests and PRs are welcome.

item.title: Formalising Federer’s Geometric Measure Theory in Rocq — project announcement
item.dc:creator: sk197876
item.description:
Hello,

I’m working on formalising the 1969 book of Federer “Geometric measure theory” in Rocq using Mathematical Components, ssreflect and Hierarchy Builder. The code is now public:

Repository sk197876/math

GitHub - sk197876/math: Formalisations of mathematical results

Formalisations of mathematical results

Actually, the whole formalisation process is done by codex using (mostly) GPT-6.1-Sol model. I’m only supervising the process. I know that Lean has a lot bigger math library but I was learning a bit of Coq during my master’s program (20 years ago) and know a little bit of it while I do not know Lean at all so I decided to use Rocq which feels more familiar to me. Anyway, I am not an expert in formalising and I am learning along the way but GPT is rather fast and now there is substantial coverage of Chapters 1 (multilinear algebra), 2 (basic measure theory), and 3 (calculus, rectifiable sets, area/coarea). I plan to check at least the statements/definitions but I’m of course very slow with that.

The aim is to follow Federer’s definitions, hypotheses and proofs as closely as possible, taking account of his erratum. One design principle is to specify mathematical objects through their laws or universal properties, prove existence separately, and hide constructions behind sealed interfaces. Subsequent proofs use the abstract laws.

The development uses MathComp’s classical foundations; it contains no admitted proofs or additional project axioms. The repository includes kernel-check and assumptions-audit records with their validation scope. I also made GPT produce documentation (docs/ dir) which gives, e.g., maps from the book to the Rocq files.

I would welcome feedback, particularly on whether the formal statements faithfully capture Federer’s mathematics, on the abstract interfaces, and on connections with existing MathComp developments. If you are interested in formalising geometric measure theory, I would be glad to discuss the project.

FRIDA 2027 - (Workshop on Formal Reasoning in Distributed Algorithms) - POPL...

FRIDA 2027, the 13th Workshop on Formal Reasoning in Distributed Algorithms, is a one-day workshop held on Monday 11 January 2027. The call for talks is open: submit a short abstract and a PDF of at most 2 pages at https://frida2027.hotcrp.com/ by...

Dear colleagues,

FRIDA brings together researchers in distributed algorithms, distributed systems, formal methods, and programming languages to discuss rigorous design and analysis of concurrent and distributed systems, from foundational theory to tool-supported verification. After 12 editions co-located with DISC, CAV, FLoC and other venues, FRIDA comes to POPL for the first time.

We invite talk proposals on topics including:

  • models of concurrent and distributed computation; fault tolerance, consensus, linearizability, and liveness
  • consistency models, weak memory models, and replicated data types
  • languages, type systems, and semantics for distributed programming
  • specification of distributed systems, including hyperproperties
  • model checking, deductive verification, and interactive theorem proving of distributed algorithms and systems
  • invariant inference, parameterized verification, and synthesis
  • runtime verification and testing of distributed systems
  • AI-assisted modeling and verification
  • tools, case studies, experience reports, and open problems

The program will combine invited and contributed talks. Contributed talks will be about 30 minutes; final slot lengths will depend on the program and will be confirmed at notification.

How to submit
Submit at https://frida2027.hotcrp.com/ :

  • the title, the authors and their affiliations, and the speaker;
  • a short abstract, to appear in the program;
  • a PDF of at most 2 pages, excluding references, in any format, describing the work and what the talk will cover.

You may optionally attach a longer document (e.g., a full paper); the PC may consult it but is not required to.

The program committee will select talks based on relevance and interest to the FRIDA audience. FRIDA has no proceedings: talks on new, ongoing, or already published work are all welcome.

Speakers are expected to present in person. We may be able to accommodate a small number of remote talks; if you may need to present remotely, please indicate this in the submission form. Talks may be recorded and, with speakers’ permission, posted online.

item.title: Package update : Small Inversions
item.dc:creator: BasileGros
item.description:
Dear all,

it is our pleasure to announce that our Rocq plugin for the automation of proxy-based small inversions has received a major update.
Here is the link to its repository:

github.com

GitHub - BasileGros/proxy-based-small-inversions: An alternative to Rocq's inversion focused on...

An alternative to Rocq's inversion focused on reducing the generated term's size and eliminating equality hypotheses.

The user interface has been greatly simplified, and there is a tutorial to both use our automated tool (covering many common cases), and also to understand the basic principles behind it. The latter are not overly complicated, once you catch the idea, so that the end user can tune them to their specific situation when needed.

As a reminder, PBSI are an inversion method that results in significantly smaller and more understandable proof and definition terms compared to the Rocq tactic inversion or the Equations package, which makes PBSI interesting in the context of dependent programming. Moreover, dependent PBSI allow to conveniently reason about such functions. To achieve this, the technique uses intermediate definitions which used to be handwritten. This package allows the user to automatically build those definitions with a simple Derive InvProxy command.

Basile Gros

item.title: PhD position at TU Delft: deriving formal languages from their semantics
item.dc:creator: benediktahrens
item.description:
PhD position at TU Delft: deriving formal languages from their semantics

I am looking for a PhD candidate for a 4-year position in the Department of Software Technology at TU Delft, funded by the Air Force Office of Scientific Research (AFOSR) and starting as soon as possible.

The project, “SemSyn: From Semantics to Syntax”, studies how to start from a specification of a class of models and derive a formal language describing them. It involves:

  • dependent type theory and its categorical semantics (categories with families, comprehension categories);
  • generalized algebraic theories;
  • Makkai’s signatures, given by inverse categories;
  • two-level type theory;
  • formalization in the Agda proof assistant, developed alongside the mathematics.

You should have a Master’s degree in mathematics, computer science, or a related field, and experience in (or a strong motivation to learn) both category theory and theoretical computer science. Experience with a proof assistant is a plus, but not required.

Applications are evaluated on a rolling basis, so please apply early rather than waiting for the deadline of 29 November 2026. I very much encourage you to get in touch with me by email (B.P.Ahrens@tudelft.nl) before, and in addition to, submitting your official application.

Sign up to be a Student Volunteer and help us make POPL 2027 a unique experience for all attendants!
POPL 2027 is pleased to offer a number of opportunities for student volunteers, who are vital to the efficient operation and continued success of the conference each year. The student volunteer program is a chance for students from around the world to participate in the conferences whilst assisting us in preparing and running the event.

The Student Volunteer Program helps more students attend the POPL conference by covering registration to the conferences, tutorials, workshops, and all associated events (but not travel or lodging expenses). In exchange for a fixed number of work hours (around 18) helping with the conference organization, you will be able to closely interact with researchers, mentors, and other students at POPL 2027. We are looking forward to seeing you in the SV team!

Eligibility

Applicants can be undergraduate, Master’s, Ph.D. full- or part-time students, of computer science or related fields, with or without previous experience as volunteers. Everyone is encouraged to apply!

Duration

Applicants must be available for at least four (4) full days between the 10th and 16th of January 2027, and will be expected to provide at least 18 hours of volunteering work in that time. Volunteers will also be expected to be available for some amount of pre-conference discussion and training if necessary.

Compensation

Every student volunteer will receive:

  • A complimentary conference registration, offering access to all open sessions (i.e., parallel paper presentations, demonstrations, and workshops) and conference proceedings.
  • Free lunches and refreshments during breaks.
  • Student volunteer garments.

Please note that Student Volunteers are responsible for their own travel and accommodation arrangements. However, Student Volunteers can apply for extra funding from SIGPLAN PAC funding or PLMW when eligible.

You can send questions about student volunteering to Celeste Barnaby (celestebarnaby@gmail.com) and Aurèle Barrière (aurele.barriere@cnrs.fr).

Applications

To apply, fill out the form on this link, before November 11th: POPL27 Student Volunteer Application .

The form is very short and won’t take more than 5 minutes to complete. We will NOT evaluate the applications in a first come first serve order.

**Deadline for submission: November 11th 2026, AoE.

item.title: Rocq bottom: a formally verified library of integer abstract domains
item.dc:creator: mlemerre
item.description:
I’m happy to announce Rocq-bottom, a new Rocq library of formally verified abstract domains, currently targeting non-relational integer abstractions. The library currently provides formally verified Intervals, Congruences, and Known Bits abstractions, some of their reduced products, together with transfer functions and refinement operators for integer expressions.

It can show, for instance, that

  • Z.lor [3,5] [4,5] ∈ [4,7],
  • Z.add 0b001? + 0b001? ∈ 0b01??,
  • for the problem x * y = 10 with 3 ≤ x ≤ 10, 1 ≤ y ≤ 10, backward multiplication can tighten the bounds to 5 ≤ x ≤ 10 and 1 ≤ y ≤ 2.

The goal of this development is not only to prove that the algorithms it contains are sound, but also that they are best (e.g., the intervals above are the tightest). All of this is developed in constructive logic, without any extra axiom. The theoretical foundations are described in the paper Rocq Bottom: Beyond Soundness with Precise Reasoning about Analysis Precision, to be published at SAS this year.

In addition, the algorithm should be efficient and practical, so that they can be integrated easily in static analyzers.

The development has reached an important first milestone, as we now have best forward and backward transfer functions over unbounded integer intervals for all the C-like integer operators (Z.add, Z.sub, Z.mul, Z.quot, Z.rem, Z.shiftl, Z.shiftr, Z.land, Z.lor, Z.lxor, Z.eqb, Z.leb, Z.ltb).

The next steps are to develop best transfer functions for the products Interval × Congruence, Interval × Congruence × Known Bits, and then build on that to build bitvector abstractions.

I’m new to Rocq and the development can probably be improved in many ways. I’d love to hear your thoughts, feedback, or suggestions!

item.title: A library for composable, extractable, partial programs
item.dc:creator: TheoWinterhalter
item.description:
It’s my pleasure to announce a new Rocq library for partial programs that was designed with Meven Lennon-Bertand and Kenji Maillard, and is now available on opam.

opam install rocq-partial

It lets you write and combine partial fixed points as follows:

Definition ack : nat → nat → partial nat :=
  #pfix ack (m : nat) (n : nat),
    match m, n with
    | 0, _ => ret (S n)
    | S m', 0 => ack m' 1
    | S m', S n' => k ← ack m n' ;; ack m' k
    end.

Definition ack_sum : nat → partial nat :=
  #pfix ack_sum n,
    if n =? 0 then ret 0
    else
      k ← lift (ack n n) ;;
      l ← ack_sum (n - 1) ;;
      ret (k + l).

It’s quite in the early stages, so there’s probably a lot missing compared to what one can find in the wild in Agda or Lean. It’s mostly driven from use cases, so if you have some that do not fit what is provided don’t hesitate to open issues or pull requests.

36th Nordic Workshop on Programming Theory
November 19-20th, 2026, University of Tartu, Tartu, Estonia
Conference web page: https://kodu.ut.ee/~nester/nwpt-2026/main.html

== Scope ==

NWPT is a series of annual regional-scope workshops on programming theory, targeted especially at younger researchers. In 2026, the workshop will take place in Tartu, Estonia. We hope this will be a nice opportunity to present recent results and/or work-in-progress, and to meet colleagues from the Nordic and Baltic countries. item.title: JFLA2027 : Dernier appel à communications
item.dc:creator: Yannick
item.description:
This message is intentionally written in French. It is a call for papers for the
“Francophone Days on Functional Languages” to be held at the end of January 2027
in Britany. Papers can be written in English, but the presentations
themselves are expected to be given in French.

Merci de faire circuler : second appel à communications

JFLA 2027 : Journées Francophones des Langages Applicatifs

jfla.eu

JFLA 2027

JFLA: JFLA 2027

26 janvier au 29 janvier 2027

Maison Saint-François

Les 38èmes Journées Francophones des Langages Applicatifs (JFLA) se tiendront
en Bretagne, à Dinard (Ille-et-Vilaine), du mardi 26 janvier 2027 au
vendredi 29 janvier 2027.

Les JFLA réunissent concepteur·rices, utilisateur·rices et théoricien·nes ;
elles ont pour ambition de couvrir les domaines des langages applicatifs, de la
preuve formelle, de la vérification de programmes, et des objets mathématiques
qui sous-tendent ces outils. Ces domaines doivent être pris au sens large : nous
souhaitons promouvoir les ponts entre les différentes thématiques.

  • Langages fonctionnels et applicatifs : sémantique, compilation, optimisation,
    typage, extensions à d’autres paradigmes.

  • Assistants de preuve : implémentation, nouvelles tactiques, développements
    présentant un intérêt théorique, technique ou méthodologique.

  • Logique, correspondance preuve-programme, réalisabilité, extraction de
    programmes, modèles.

  • Spécification, prototypage, développements formels d’algorithmes.

  • Vérification de programmes ou de modèles, vérification déductive,
    interprétation abstraite, raffinement.

  • Utilisation industrielle des langages fonctionnels et applicatifs,
    ou des méthodes issues de la communauté scientifique. Outils et
    plateformes pour le web.

  • Enseignement ou diffusion des langages fonctionnels et
    applicatifs. Environnements et méthodes de développement, retours
    d’expérience.

Les articles soumis aux JFLA sont relus par au moins deux personnes s’ils sont
acceptés, et au moins trois personnes s’ils sont rejetés. Les critiques du
comité de programme sont toujours bienveillantes et la plupart du temps
encourageantes et constructives, même en cas de rejet.

Il n’y a donc pas de raison de ne pas soumettre aux JFLA !

DATES IMPORTANTES

/!\ Attention : les dates limites sont fermes et définitives.
Il n’y aura pas d’extension. /!\

  • Soumission des résumés et articles : 16 octobre 2026, GMT+2
  • Notification aux auteurs et autrices : 2 décembre 2026, GMT+2
  • Version finale des articles : 16 décembre 2026, GMT+2

SOUMISSIONS

Nous acceptons deux types de soumissions :

  • Article de recherche (18 pages max.) portant sur des travaux originaux. Nous
    acceptons des travaux en cours, pour lesquels l’aspect recherche n’est pas
    entièrement finalisé. Nous encourageons aussi la soumission d’articles
    présentant avec élégance un résultat connu sous un angle nouveau.

  • Article court (9 pages max.) décrivant un problème particulier, les pistes en
    cours d’investigation, et visant à rechercher de l’aide de la part de la
    communauté. Les articles courts peuvent également présenter de manière
    synthétique et cohérente des résultats déjà publiés. Enfin, ils peuvent
    présenter un outil logiciel dont l’exposé constituera une démonstration.

CONSIGNES AUX AUTEURS ET AUTRICES

Les articles peuvent être rédigés en français ou en anglais.

La forme de l’article doit être soignée, et le contenu rédigé de manière
structurée et claire.

Le style LaTeX jflart doit impérativement être utilisé sans modification de la
mise en page. Le style LaTeX et sa documentation sont disponibles depuis le site
web de la conférence.

NEW Soumissions écrites à l’aide de Typst et non LaTeX sont bienvenues !
Nous n’avons pas encore de template officiel pour Typst, mais nous en fournirons un dès que possible.

Les limites de pages sont strictes. Les références bibliographiques ne sont pas
comptabilisées dans la limite de pages. Les annexes aux articles ne sont pas
autorisées.

Les auteurs et autrices peuvent soumettre du matériel supplémentaire, séparé de
l’article soumis, sous forme de texte (version longue, sans limite de pages)
et/ou de développement logiciel. L’évaluation de ce matériel supplémentaire est
à la discrétion du comité de programme. Les articles soumis doivent donc être
auto-contenus et évaluables sans ce matériel supplémentaire.

Les soumissions parallèles dans d’autres conférences, journaux ou workshops avec
actes ne sont pas autorisées.

Les membres du comité de programme sont autorisés à soumettre un article. Les
présidentes du comité ne le sont pas.

Les articles doivent être soumis via le site :

types-hotcrp.paris.inria.fr

JFLA 2027

L’évaluation des articles suit un processus en simple-aveugle : les rapports
des articles sont anonymes, mais pas les auteurs et autrices.

Les articles acceptés seront publiés dans les actes de la conférence, sur HAL,
et les auteurs et autrices en donneront une présentation lors des journées. Les
présentations seront, de préférence, données en français.

Yannick ZAKOWSKI et Stefania DUMBRAVA
JFLA 2027

Research positions in seL4, formal verification and AI-assisted theorem proving for agentic security at the University of Melbourne

The University of Melbourne is recruiting Postdoctoral Research Fellows / Research Fellows / Senior Research Fellows to work on the Agentic-seL4 project (https://agentic-sel4.github.io), an international collaboration with the Universities of Surrey and Sheffield.

The project is developing formally verified mechanisms on top of seL4 for securely containing AI agents, together with AI-assisted verification techniques and proof agents for maintaining and extending large-scale Isabelle/HOL developments.

We are interested in candidates with expertise in one or more of interactive theorem proving, formal verification, seL4, information-flow/security foundations, automated reasoning, or AI-assisted theorem proving. Dear Colleagues,

We are looking to recruit a Research Fellow at the University of
Sheffield, UK, for a new project on formal verification with Isabelle,
funded by the Advanced Research + Invention Agency (ARIA).

The project, jointly undertaken with the University of Surrey and the
University of Melbourne, will develop a formally verified reference
monitor on top of seL4 for the secure containment of AI agents,
including mechanisms for dynamically controlling agents’ capabilities
and information flows. It will also use AI techniques to accelerate
large-scale formal verification, trained on the seL4 proof base.

The position is at Grade 8 (UK Lecturer level), with a salary of
£53,301–£58,225, and is initially for 14 months. We have substantial
funding for access to state-of-the-art AI models and computing
infrastructure. We are interested in candidates with expertise in
interactive theorem proving, formal verification, information-flow
security, seL4, and optionally neurosymbolic AI and AI-assisted
reasoning. Candidates do not need to cover all these areas. Particular
preference will be given to candidates with strong Isabelle expertise
(or substantial experience with related interactive theorem provers),

would also be very interested in hearing from excellent Isabelle
researchers who may be at an earlier career stage than would normally

item.dc:creator: sattler
item.description:
TYPES 2026: Post-proceedings Call for Papers

types2026.cse.chalmers.se

TYPES 2026: Post-proceedings

TYPES is a major forum for the presentation of research on all aspects of type theory and its applications. TYPES 2026 was held from 4 to 8 May 2026 at Chalmers University of Technology and University of Gothenburg. The post-proceedings volume will be published in LIPIcs, Leibniz International Proceedings in Informatics, an open-access series of conference proceedings.

Submission Guidelines

Submission is open to everyone, also to those who did not participate in the TYPES 2026 conference. We welcome high-quality descriptions of original work, as well as position papers, overview papers, and system descriptions. Submissions should be written in English, and be original, i.e., neither previously published, nor simultaneously submitted to a journal or a conference.

  • Formatting: Papers have to be formatted with the current LIPIcs style and adhere to the style requirements of LIPIcs.

  • Page limits: The upper limit for the length of submissions is 20 pages for the main text (including appendices, but excluding title page and bibliography).

  • Supplementary material: Authors have the option to attach to their submission a zip or tgz file containing code (formalised proofs or programs), but reviewers are not obliged to take the attachments into account, and they will not be published.

Submission site: TYPES 2026 Postproceedings

Deadlines

  • Submission of title and abstract: 16 November 2026 AoE
  • Submission of full paper: 30 November 2026 AoE
  • Author notification: 30 March 2027 AoE

Topics of interest

The scope of the post-proceedings is the same as the scope of the conference: the theory and practice of type theory. In particular, we welcome submissions on the following topics:

  • foundations of type theory and constructive mathematics;
  • applications of type theory;
  • dependently typed programming;
  • industrial uses of type theory technology;
  • meta-theoretic studies of type systems;
  • proof assistants and proof technology;
  • automation in computer-assisted reasoning;
  • formalizing mathematics using type theory;
  • links between type theory and
    • functional programming;
    • homotopy theory;
    • linguistics;
    • machine learning.

Editors

Andreas Abel and Christian Sattler
Chalmers University of Technology and University of Gothenburg, Sweden

Workshop Overview

The series of RocqPL (formerly CoqPL) workshops provide an opportunity for programming languages researchers and practitioners with an interest in the Rocq Prover to meet and interact with one another and members from the core Rocq development team.   • Formalizations of PL research in Rocq
  • General purpose libraries and tactic language extensions
  • Domain-specific libraries for programming language formalization and verification
  • IDEs, profilers, tracers, debuggers, and testing tools
  • Reports on ongoing proof efforts conducted via (or in the context of) the Rocq Prover
  • Experience reports from Rocq usage in educational or industrial contexts

Workshop Format

The workshop format will be driven by you, the members of the community. We will solicit abstracts for talks and proposals for demonstrations and flesh out format details based on responses. We expect the final program to include experiment reports, panel discussions, and invited talks (details TBA). Talks will be selected according to relevance to the workshop, based on the submission of an extended abstract.

To foster open discussion of cutting edge research which can later be published in full conference proceedings, we will not publish papers from the workshop. However, presentations may be recorded and the videos may be made publicly available.
